title: Free novice program for hypertrophy
summary: Presents his free 3-day (Mon/Wed/Fri) novice hypertrophy template: one main compound per day (squat, bench, deadlift), a variation of another compound, high-frequency pull-ups and push-ups, and a few accessories. He explains rep ranges (low/medium/high), sets, autoregulated progression, and stresses that it's a template meant to build discipline, work capacity and the ability to program for yourself.

claims.claim: The program is three days a week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday), each session taking about an hour to an hour and a half.

Monday: squats (any knee-dominant compound with triple extension, e.g. high bar, front, SSB, low bar, lunges) for 1-3 heavy sets of 4-8 reps; then a full-ROM deadlift variation supersetted with pull-ups, 4 sets of 6-10/AMRAP; then skull crushers supersetted with hammer curls, 4 x 8-12; then push-ups and abs to AMRAP.

Wednesday: bench (replaceable by dips or push-ups) 1-3 heavy sets of 4-8 plus 3+ back-off sets of 6-10; overhead press supersetted with chin-ups 4 x 6-10/AMRAP; hyperextensions or cable rows 4 x 8-12; abs AMRAP.
Friday: deadlifts 1-3 heavy sets of 2-5; squat variation supersetted with pull-ups 4 x 6-10; EZ bar curls supersetted with pull-ups 4 x 8-12/AMRAP; push-ups and abs AMRAP.
Outside the three main lifts and their variations, novices shouldn't swap exercises unless they understand variations and muscle activation, since not every lift is equivalent.
If you can't do pull-ups, do negatives: jump to the top and lower yourself slowly.
The program uses high-frequency, low-volume pull-ups (many sets of 2-3) because novices can usually do only about 5, and this builds the ability fast.

Benching once a week is not enough for strength or size, so bench day has slightly more volume and the rest of the horizontal pressing comes from push-ups on Monday and Friday, done until you can't get 3-4 reps in a row.

Squat and deadlift are each trained twice a week with lots of time between: heavy squat Monday and squat accessory Friday, heavy deadlift Friday and deadlift accessory Monday, with the weekend to recover from lower body.
Upper body gets more frequency because those areas respond well to training every two days and are less taxing; pull-ups and push-ups are barely taxing.
Start with any weight, even the empty bar; the goal is to accumulate lots of quality reps, never struggling or compromising your ability to come back next session.
What matters most for a novice is building the discipline of coming in three times a week; motivation doesn't work in bodybuilding, routine does.
Not doing every compound several times a week is a weakness for strength progression, but the program aims to build work capacity, not weight on the bar.
Volume starts very low but grows until you do more than most people on 5x5 programs, producing more tonnage and better work capacity later.
He has never followed someone else's program; a self-written program may not be optimal but is most suitable and you learn from its mistakes.
Paying for a program is a waste of money, especially for a novice.

If you swap a main lift (e.g. front squats, dips, Jefferson deadlifts), swap its accessory accordingly (paused/pin front squats, Jefferson block pulls); default accessories are paused squats and deficit deadlifts.
Even if you replace bench with push-ups, keep push-ups as the horizontal accessory rather than benching three times a week, which taxes the shoulders.
At least one vertical press per week is non-negotiable; the overhead press needs no accessory at first, and just doing it puts you ahead of most novices.

Accessories: skull crushers for the triceps long head, hammer curls for forearms, hyperextensions for lower back health and hamstrings, chin-ups for biceps; keep the pull-ups because they're great for back, spine and shoulder health and not taxing.
Novices don't need arm days or much arm isolation, but some isolation gives them a taste of it.
Rear delts, traps and calves are left out so as not to overpack the program; novices lack the mental capacity and recovery to stay in the gym for three hours.
Pick three rep ranges: low, medium, high. His own: low 2-5 for some lifts or 4-8, medium 6-10, high 8-12 or 10-15.
A higher-volume novice setup: 4-8 low, 6-10 medium, 8-12 high; aim for the bottom of the range, repeat until you can add a rep, progressing through the range.

Do the main compound in the low range, the accessory in the medium range, and isolation in the high range; the main compound can use any rep range, but accessories never go low and isolations always stay high.
He does 1-3 heavy sets on the compound and 4 sets for everything else, up to 6 sets for isolation if you want.

Sets are the volume variable and are easier to manipulate once reps are established; if you feel good after the heavy sets you can add four more, but don't go overboard on the opener and save energy for accessories.
Mistakes are fine for novices as long as they stay in a safe rep range with good form; they won't get injured.

When you hit the top reps of your range comfortably several times, add weight: 5 lbs per side is a conservative increase; 2.5 lbs per side for overhead press and curls. Alternatively drop weight and change rep range.
Think for yourself rather than being a drone following a carved path; respecting the compounds/accessories/isolations template forges innovation and discipline for a decades-long journey.
